info.text: Quiz: 20 questions (multiple choice, code tracing, drag and drop).

questiontext.text: Which line lights bit k of x without changing any other bit?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. OR with a mask that has a single lit bit forces that bit to 1 and leaves every other bit alone. Plain assignment would erase all the other bits.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int x = 13;
x |= 2;
x &= ~8;
x ^= 1;
cout << x << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 13 is 1101. Setting bit 1 gives 1111 (15). Clearing bit 3 gives 0111 (7). Flipping bit 0 gives 0110, which is 6.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this code print?

main.cpp
int x = 12;
cout << (x & (x - 1)) << endl;

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 12 is 1100 and 11 is 1011. Combining them with & leaves 1000: the lowest lit bit of 12 has been removed.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

name.text: Q04 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct symbol into the gap so the program prints 4 (the lowest lit bit of 12).

main.cpp
int x = 12;
cout << (x & [[1]]x) << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. x & -x keeps only the lowest lit bit: 12 is 1100, so the result is 0100, which is 4. With ~x the result would be 0, and !x is 0 for any non-zero x.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int x = 12;
cout << (x & -x) << endl;

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
for (int x : {16, 18, 0, 1}) {
    cout << (x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0);
}
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 16 and 1 are powers of two, so they print 1. 18 is 10010, which has two lit bits, so it prints 0. Zero is rejected by x > 0. The output is 1001.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Why must the power-of-two test include x > 0?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Zero has no lit bits, so removing the lowest lit bit leaves 0 and the test passes. Zero is not a power of two, so we must exclude it explicitly.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Because 0 & -1 is 0, so zero would wrongly pass the test (x & (x - 1)) == 0
Because negative numbers are powers of two

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines so the program prints 8 (it removes the lowest lit bit of 12 using the isolated bit).

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]
 2  [[2]]
 3  [[3]]
 4  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. x must exist first. low is computed from x (it is 4). XOR-ing x with its lowest lit bit removes that bit, and the print comes last.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int x = 12;
int low = x & -x;
x ^= low;
cout << x << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each expression with its purpose.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

x & (x - 1)  →  [[1]]

x & -x  →  [[2]]

(x >> k) & 1  →  [[3]]

x ^= (1 << k)  →  [[4]]

(1 << k) - 1  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Each trick is a single expression. Learn these five and you can read most bit-manipulation code.

The correct answer:

  • x & (x - 1) → Removes the lowest lit bit
  • x & -x → Keeps only the lowest lit bit
  • (x >> k) & 1 → Reads bit k as 0 or 1
  • x ^= (1 << k) → Flips bit k
  • (1 << k) - 1 → Gives k lit bits from the bottom

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int x = 40;
cout << __builtin_popcount(x) << " " << __builtin_ctz(x) << " " << (x & -x) << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 40 is 101000. It has two lit bits (popcount 2), three zeros at the end (ctz 3), and its lowest lit bit is worth 8.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Which line switches bit k off without changing any other bit?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. ~(1 << k) has a 0 at bit k and 1 everywhere else, so & clears that bit and keeps all the others.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Sort each expression: does it change x, or only read it?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

x |= 4;  →  [[1]]

x &= x - 1;  →  [[1]]

x ^= 1;  →  [[1]]

(x >> 2) & 1  →  [[2]]

x & -x  →  [[2]]

x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Compound assignments such as |=, &= and ^= modify x. The other expressions only compute a value from x and leave it untouched.

The correct answer:

Changes x: x |= 4;, x &= x - 1;, x ^= 1;
Only reads x: (x >> 2) & 1, x & -x, x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0

questiontext.text:
What does this code print?

main.cpp
cout << (13 & (1 << 3)) << endl;

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 13 is 1101, and 1 << 3 is 1000. Their AND is 1000, which is 8 and not 1. This is why x & (1 << k) should be used as a condition, not as a 0-or-1 value.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
const int READ = 1, WRITE = 2, EXEC = 4;
int p = READ | WRITE;
p &= ~READ;
p |= EXEC;
cout << p << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. READ | WRITE is 3 (011). Removing READ leaves 010. Adding EXEC gives 110, which is 6.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

name.text: Q14 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct operators into the gaps so the program prints 5.

main.cpp
int x = 15;
x [[1]] ~(1 << 1);
x [[2]] (1 << 3);
cout << x << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. 15 is 1111. &= ~(1 << 1) clears bit 1 and gives 1101 (13). ^= (1 << 3) then flips bit 3 and gives 0101, which is 5. Using |= would not clear or flip anything.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int x = 15;
x &= ~(1 << 1);
x ^= (1 << 3);
cout << x << endl;

questiontext.text:
Arrange the steps of the power-of-two test for a number x.

Drag the steps into the correct order.

1. [[1]]

2. [[2]]

3. [[3]]

4. [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. First rule out zero, then compute x - 1, combine it with x to remove the lowest lit bit, and finally check whether anything is left.

The correct answer:

  1. Make sure x is greater than zero
  2. Compute x - 1
  3. Combine x and x - 1 with &
  4. Check whether the result is zero

questiontext.text:
Match each word with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Mask  →  [[1]]

Flag  →  [[2]]

Popcount  →  [[3]]

Toggle  →  [[4]]

Lowest set bit  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These are the words you will hear whenever people talk about bit tricks.

The correct answer:

  • Mask → A number built to select particular bits
  • Flag → A single bit that stands for one option
  • Popcount → The number of lit bits
  • Toggle → Turning a bit into its opposite
  • Lowest set bit → The smallest lit position in a number

questiontext.text:
Sort each task by the line that does it.

Drag the correct label next to every item.

Turn a lamp on  →  [[1]]

Grant a permission  →  [[1]]

Turn a lamp off  →  [[2]]

Revoke a permission  →  [[2]]

Enable a feature flag  →  [[1]]

Clear an error flag  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Setting a bit uses OR with the mask. Clearing a bit uses AND with the inverted mask. Granting and enabling are "set" operations; revoking and clearing are "clear" operations.

The correct answer:

x |= mask: Turn a lamp on, Grant a permission, Enable a feature flag
x &= ~mask: Turn a lamp off, Revoke a permission, Clear an error flag

questiontext.text:
What does this loop print?

main.cpp
int x = 255, steps = 0;
while (x) {
    x &= x - 1;
    steps++;
}
cout << steps << endl;

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Each pass of x &= x - 1 removes exactly one lit bit. The number 255 has eight lit bits, so the loop runs eight times.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int x = 53;
cout << (x & ((1 << 3) - 1)) << " " << (x >> 3) << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 53 is 110101. The mask (1 << 3) - 1 is 111, so the low three bits 101 give 5. Shifting right by 3 removes them and leaves 110, which is 6.
